title: NASA-UAP-VM005, Apollo 12, 1969
summary: This image is a processed version of an Apollo 12 lunar surface photograph (1969) in which five areas above the horizon have been digitally cropped and magnified to highlight small luminous anomalies visible in the lunar sky. The image has been editorially annotated with yellow boxes and labels (Area 1 through Area 5) to direct viewer attention to points of light or luminous objects above the lunar horizon. The document's provenance and analytical authority are explicitly disclaimed in the accompanying context blurb.
key_findings: Five areas of interest labeled Area 1 through Area 5 are highlighted above the lunar horizon in an Apollo 12 surface photograph from 1969. | Area 5 contains the most visually distinctive anomaly, appearing as an elongated, multi-toned luminous object (white and light blue) against the dark lunar sky. | Areas 1, 2, 3, and 4 contain smaller point-like or clustered luminous features that are less distinctly shaped. | The image has been explicitly acknowledged as modified from its original state for contextual illustration purposes, not as an investigative or analytical determination. | No classification markings, originating agency analysis, or official UAP determination language appears on this document.
credibility_notes: The accompanying context blurb explicitly states the image has been modified from its original state and that such alterations do not constitute analytical judgment or factual determination. The anomalies in Areas 1–4 are extremely small and indistinct at the resolution shown; they are consistent with stars, film artifacts, lens flare, or cosmic ray hits on film. Area 5's elongated object could similarly be a film defect, overexposed star, or orbital hardware. No original unmodified source image, EXIF data, film negative reference, or NASA photographic archive catalog number is provided for verification. Single-image evidence with no corroborating sensor data or witness accounts.

title: Western US Event
summary: This document summarizes four distinct UAP incidents reported by six to seven federal law enforcement special agents (USPER1 through USPER7) over a two-day period in the Western United States in 2023. The incidents include orange orbs launching smaller red orbs, a large stationary luminous orb estimated at 12-18 meters in diameter, a low-flying triangular/kite-shaped object observed on the ground, and a second transparent kite-shaped object observed approximately 30 minutes later. AARO assessed these reports as among the most compelling in its current holdings, though no technical sensor data was directly collected during the events.

title: NASA-UAP-D007, Skylab Technical Crew Debriefing 1973
summary: This document contains excerpts from three Skylab technical crew debriefings (Skylab 2, 3, and 4) conducted between June 1973 and February 1974, covering unusual visual phenomena observed by astronauts during their missions. The excerpts include: crew-reported light flashes (Skylab 2), a bright reddish rotating object in a similar orbit (Skylab 3), and flashing lights with relative motion (Skylab 4). In all cases, the crews offered mundane or speculative explanations, including cosmic particle strikes on the retina, other satellites, and debris from Skylab itself.
key_findings: Skylab 2 crew (Conrad, Kerwin, Weitz) all reported seeing internal light flashes, most likely cosmic ray/particle strikes on the retina, possibly correlated with the South Atlantic Anomaly. | Skylab 3 crew (Garriott, Lousma, Bean) observed a bright reddish rotating object in a very similar orbit for approximately 10 minutes; its identity was never explained to the crew and they formally requested identification. | The Skylab 3 object was estimated to be no more than 30-50 nautical miles distant based on its 5-7 second delay entering Earth's shadow relative to Skylab, and had a brightness variation with a 10-second rotation period. | Skylab 4 Commander Gerald Carr reported two or three sightings of flashing lights outside with definite relative motion, presumed to be Skylab debris or other satellites; one or two appeared to be tumbling. | No crew in any of the three debriefings concluded that the observed phenomena were anomalous beyond conventional explanations, though the Skylab 3 satellite remained officially unidentified at time of debriefing.
official_conclusion: Unresolved for Skylab 3 object; Skylab 4 lights presumed to be Skylab debris or other satellites; Skylab 2 light flashes presumed to be cosmic particle retinal interactions
credibility_notes: The light flashes reported by Skylab 2 crew are well-understood as cosmic ray interactions with the retina, not external phenomena. The Skylab 3 reddish rotating object, while unidentified at debriefing, was assessed by the crew themselves as 'obviously a satellite' based on its orbital behavior, rotation period, and proximity; the crew's own framing is mundane. Skylab 4 flashing lights were presumed by Commander Carr to be Skylab debris or other satellites. All observations are single-mission visual-only with no sensor corroboration. No official identification of the Skylab 3 object is present in these excerpts.
incident_duration: approximately 5 to 10 minutes (Skylab 3 object); recurring over mission duration (Skylab 2 light flashes and Skylab 4 flashing lights)
historical_significance: Three successive NASA astronaut crews aboard Skylab (1973-1974) formally reported unidentified visual phenomena in their official technical debriefings, including a bright rotating reddish object in near-identical orbit whose identification was never supplied to the crew despite their formal request.

title: DOW-UAP-D019, Mission Report, Syria, February 21, 2023
summary: This is a declassified SECRET//NOFORN Mission Report (MISREP) filed by the 389th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron (389 EFS), 332nd Air Expeditionary Wing, documenting a 2-ship F-15E DCA (Defensive Counter Air) mission flown on February 20-21, 2023, out of Muwaffaq Salti Air Base (OJMS), Jordan, under Operation Inherent Resolve. During the mission, aircrew observed three possible UAPs and one possible balloon in the vicinity of Shaddadi, Syria, and also experienced multifunction terminal (MFT) radar jamming. The document was declassified on 8 October 2025 by MG Richard A. Harrison, USCENTCOM Chief of Staff, and approved for release to AARO.
key_findings: At 0025Z on 21 February 2023, aircrew observed 3x possible UAPs in the vicinity of Shaddadi at FL240; no radar returns were received from the UAPs and 2 white objects were noted as IR significant; a WSV (Weapon System Video) was produced. | At 0021Z-0024Z, the flight received MFT radar jamming in the vicinity of Shaddadi at FL270 lasting 3 minutes, partially affecting the APG-82 radar system in the 8.8-9.9GHz frequency band; the working theory is that it was caused by a Turkish X-band jammer near the Syria/Turkey border. | At 0135Z, aircrew observed 1x possible balloon in the vicinity of Shaddadi at FL210; a WSV was produced; no further information was reported. | The crew reported no radar returns received from the UAPs and no health effects experienced by aircrew during the UAP observation. | The total mission time was 4 hours 55 minutes with 3 hours 37 minutes on station; the mission was not flown as originally fragged due to mission amendments.
official_conclusion: NFTR (Nothing Further To Report); no radar returns received from UAP; no health effects to aircrew; WSV produced.
credibility_notes: The UAP observation is visual/IR only with no radar returns confirmed, and the document explicitly notes 'NFTR' (Nothing Further To Report) for the UAP sightings. The three UAP objects are labeled 'possible' and no shape, size, or movement characteristics are described beyond being IR-significant white objects. The concurrent radar jamming event has a proposed mundane explanation (Turkish X-band jammer). The second sighting is labeled 'possible balloon.' Witness type is human aircrew; WSV (weapon system video) was reportedly produced but is not included in this document. Coordinates are redacted.

title: NASA-UAP-D006, Apollo 17 Technical Crew Debriefing, 1973
summary: This is an excerpt from the Apollo 17 Technical Crew Debriefing dated January 4, 1973, prepared by NASA's Training Office, Crew Training and Simulation Division at the Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston, Texas. The excerpt (page 24-4) contains statements from astronauts Evans, Cernan, and Schmitt regarding unusual visual phenomena observed during the mission, including light flashes experienced throughout the flight and a fireball sighting during reentry/recovery.

title: 65_HS1-834228961_62-HQ-83894_Serial_164
summary: This document is Air Intelligence Requirements Memorandum Number 4, dated 15 February 1949, issued by the Directorate of Intelligence, Headquarters United States Air Force. It establishes formal Air Force requirements and standardized reporting procedures for sightings of unconventional aircraft and unidentified flying objects, including 'Flying Discs.' The document supersedes earlier Army collection memoranda and distributes reporting protocols to all major Air Commands, Air Attaches, and non-Air Force agencies including the FBI, CIA, and naval intelligence. The file contains approximately 15-16 identical copies of the same 7-page memorandum, filed as FBI case 62-HQ-83894, Serial 164.
key_findings: The USAF formally established continuing intelligence requirements for UFO/unconventional aircraft sightings as early as 15 February 1949, signed by Major General C.P. Cabell, Director of Intelligence. | The memorandum superseded Department of the Army Collection Memorandum Number 7 (21 January 1948) and letter CSGID 425.1 (25 March 1948), indicating Army had jurisdiction before Air Force took over UFO reporting. | All sighting reports were to be transmitted to Commanding General, Air Materiel Command, Wright-Patterson AFB, Dayton, Ohio, Attn: MCIAXO-3, establishing Wright-Patterson as the central collection point. | The memorandum required investigators to check surfaces with Geiger counters for radioactivity and collect soil samples if objects contacted earth, indicating serious physical evidence collection protocols. | Distribution included the Director of Central Intelligence, Chief of Naval Intelligence, Director of the FBI, Department of State, and US Coast Guard, demonstrating the multi-agency scope of early UAP reporting infrastructure.
official_conclusion: Procedural memorandum establishing collection requirements; no incident conclusion applicable.
credibility_notes: This document contains no incident-specific UAP content; it is a procedural memorandum establishing reporting requirements. The file consists of approximately 15-16 near-identical copies of the same 7-page memo, which is administratively redundant. The memorandum describes what information to collect but does not itself constitute evidence of any UAP incident.

title: 18_100754_ General 1946-7_Vol_2
summary: This multi-document package contains a collection of classified memoranda and correspondence from 1947 between the Air Materiel Command (AMC), Army Air Forces (AAF), and related intelligence offices concerning 'Flying Discs' and 'Flying Saucers.' The centerpiece is the famous Twining Memorandum of 23 September 1947, in which Lieutenant General N.F. Twining formally assessed that the flying disc phenomenon is real, not visionary, and recommended establishment of a formal study project. Additional documents include follow-up memos, a photograph debunking case, and early organizational steps toward what became Project Sign.
key_findings: Lieutenant General N.F. Twining's 23 September 1947 memorandum formally concluded that the flying disc phenomenon 'is something real and not visionary or fictitious,' describing objects approximately disc-shaped, metallic or light-reflecting, flying at speeds above 300 knots, with extreme maneuverability including evasive action when contacted by friendly aircraft or radar. | On 30 December 1947, Major General L.C. Craigie directed AMC to establish a formal project to collect, collate, evaluate, and distribute information on atmospheric sightings of national security concern, assigned Priority 2A with 'Restricted' security classification and the code name 'Sign.' | Colonel Robert Taylor's August 1947 routing sheet formally asked the Deputy Chief of Air Staff for Research and Development to confirm whether any classified U.S. research project matched the flying saucer description; Major General Curtis E. LeMay responded on 29 August 1947 that 'The Army Air Forces has no research project with the characteristics described.' | Photographs submitted by civilian Mary L. Herren from Portland, Oregon — allegedly taken November 1946 near Jefferson, Oregon — were assessed by HQ USAF intelligence as likely film or camera defects rather than flying discs, and no further investigation was requested. | AMC intelligence considered three possible origins for the objects: domestic high-security project unknown to AC/AS-2, foreign nation with nuclear propulsion capability, or natural phenomena; the lack of physical crash-recovered evidence was explicitly noted as a limitation.
official_conclusion: The phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious; objects probably approximate the shape of a disc and exhibit extreme rates of climb and maneuverability; origin undetermined pending further investigation.
credibility_notes: This is an analytical assessment based on aggregated witness reports with no sensor corroboration documented in these pages; Twining explicitly acknowledged the lack of physical evidence. One photograph case was dismissed as film defects. The Mrs. Merchant theory (Russian launch from Mexico) was assessed as unworthy of further investigation. The documents represent official conclusions drawn from secondary witness interrogation data, not direct observation by the signatories.

title: NASA-UAP-D002, Apollo 17 Transcript, 1972
summary: This document comprises excerpts from the Apollo 17 Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription (December 1972), covering three separate observation periods in which crew members reported anomalous visual phenomena: bright tumbling particles near the spacecraft on Day 1, multiple flashing rotating objects at distance on Day 2, and a brief flash on the lunar surface on Day 3. official_conclusion: No official UAP conclusion stated; crew members proposed mundane explanations including spacecraft debris, ice fragments, paint, separated rocket stage (S-IVB), SLA panels, and meteorite impact for respective observations.

The Day 2 flashing object sightings are visual-only with no sensor corroboration. CDR Cernan's initial light flash observation occurred while he was in a self-described 'sleep-hazy mode,' significantly reducing its evidential value. title: DOW-UAP-D094, Analysis of Flying Object Incidents in the United States, 1949

The document concludes that some type of flying object has been observed but that definitive identification and origin cannot be established, while warning that foreign (Soviet) origin cannot be ruled out and would constitute a national security threat.

title: DOE-UAP-D004, Los Alamos Conference on Aerial Phenomena, 1949
summary: This document is a full 24-page transcript of a classified SECRET conference held on February 16, 1949, at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, convened to analyze a series of anomalous 'green fireball' sightings reported over atomic weapons installations in New Mexico. The attendees included leading Manhattan Project scientists (Teller, Bradbury, Manley, Reines) alongside military intelligence officers, FBI, and meteor expert Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, who led the technical briefing. No consensus explanation was reached, and LaPaz explicitly stated the phenomena were inconsistent with conventional meteorite falls in multiple key characteristics.
key_findings: Dr. Lincoln LaPaz concluded that the green fireballs, observed traveling nearly horizontal paths at 8-10 mile altitudes across distances of 25-100+ miles, were 'not conventional meteor falls' based on their unique color (~5200 angstrom yellow-green), constant angular velocity, absence of sound, absence of recovered fragments, and absence of animal disturbance. | At least 10 incidents were confirmed by sufficient independent observers as analogs to the 'Starvation Peak' green fireball of December 12, 1948, with approximately 20 additional lower-confidence sightings. | The green fireballs were concentrated geographically near atomic bomb installations including Los Alamos, Sandia Base, and White Sands, a pattern LaPaz noted and suggested could indicate 'defensive maneuvers of a higher U.S. Command,' though he was rebuked for this suggestion. | Captain Neef disclosed that Project Sign had been renamed Project Grudge, and that the New Mexico green fireball phenomena had been included within its scope; the Air Force was identified as the primary gathering and reporting agency for these phenomena. | Dr. Edward Teller performed blackboard calculations on light, speed, kinetic energy, and shock wave characteristics and concluded the phenomena 'ought to be a material body' but might alternatively be 'an electron phenomenon,' while noting the absence of sound at the observed speed was theoretically incompatible with a solid object of appreciable size.
official_conclusion: No consensus reached; phenomena determined to be inconsistent with conventional meteorite falls but no alternative explanation confirmed; project transferred to Project Grudge for continued investigation.
credibility_notes: The phenomena are discussed as potentially meteoric in origin throughout the conference, and Dr. Bradbury and Dr. Teller both resist dismissing conventional meteor explanations outright. All observations described are visual/witness-only with no sensor corroboration obtained; the photographic patrol on December 19 recorded nothing. LaPaz's personal sighting was single-station and could not yield a full trajectory determination. The conference reached no consensus and produced no actionable physical evidence. Audio recording was repeatedly interrupted by a ditch digger outside, causing gaps in the transcript.

title: DOW-UAP-D097, Project Sign Progress Report, 1948
summary: This is the initial progress report for Project Sign (Project HT-304), dated 23 April 1948, submitted by Headquarters Air Materiel Command (Wright-Patterson AFB) to the USAF Chief of Staff. It consolidates 100 UFO incident reports from mid-1946 through early 1948, providing tabulated data on locations, observer occupations, object descriptions, maneuvers, speeds, and altitudes. Enclosures include photographs from Incident #40, a photographic analysis memo, and a multi-part article from 'The Aeroplane' periodical on low aspect ratio disc-wing aircraft ('The Biology of the Flying Saucer').
key_findings: Objects were described as oval, disc, or saucer-shaped in 31 of the 100 reported incidents, with reported sizes ranging from a 25-cent piece to 250 feet in diameter and up to the bulk of six B-29 airplanes. | Observed behaviors included high rates of climb, hovering for considerable lengths of time, and speeds ranging from very slow to supersonic across the 100 incidents. | Dr. Irving Langmuir of General Electric Research Laboratories concluded that available data was insufficient for positive identification and was reluctant to accept flying discs as a reality. | AMC headquarters assessed that it was technically possible to construct a low aspect ratio aircraft replicating the appearance and performance of reported flying discs, achievable through boundary layer control. | Two specific incidents were discredited: Incident #18 was definitively determined to be a hoax perpetrated for publicity and money, and the reporter of Incident #84 was assessed as an excitable person with an exaggerated imagination.

summary: This is Air Intelligence Division Study No. 203, dated 10 December 1948, jointly produced by USAF and ONI (DI/USAF-ONI). official_conclusion: It must be accepted that some type of flying objects have been observed, although their identification and origin are not discernible. In the interest of national defense it would be unwise to overlook the possibility that some of these objects may be of foreign origin.

It is a theoretical physics survey examining the concept of 'vacuum' or 'spacetime metric' engineering as a potential basis for advanced aerospace propulsion, drawing on general relativity to catalog physical effects that would theoretically result from engineered spacetime modifications. Its connection to AAWSAP is notable for program-context purposes, but its content is purely theoretical.

title: DOW-UAP-D156, Air Intelligence Information Report, Guam, 1956
summary: Air Intelligence Information Report (IR-7-57, dated 8 Feb 57) documenting a 31 Dec 1956 night sighting by an F-86D pilot over Guam of a round, blinking white light that reportedly maneuvered with and circled the interceptor for about 10 minutes. A lighted weather balloon had been launched earlier, but the preparing officer concluded the balloon could explain the sighting only if it had malfunctioned and stayed at low altitude.
key_findings: F-86D pilot (1st Lt Ted Brunson, 41st Fighter-Interceptor Squadron) reported a round, dime-sized blinking white light at 1610Z on 31 Dec 1956 over the Guam radio range holding pattern at about 26,000 ft MSL. | The pilot reported the object turned with his aircraft, could not be closed with even in afterburner, climbed from 20,000 to 30,000 ft, and circled the interceptor twice over about 10 minutes before he broke off for low fuel. | A lighted weather balloon launched at 1432Z by the U.S. Weather Bureau at the U.S. Navy Communications Station was last tracked 5 miles west at 20,000 ft at 1500Z, with a slower-than-normal ascent rate. | The preparing officer stated a normally ascending balloon would have been much higher than the sighting altitude; a malfunctioning balloon that leveled off or descended could possibly explain it. | The pilot, questioned again, rejected the balloon explanation because the object maneuvered with the F-86D and accelerated past his aircraft; no other air traffic was known, verified by checks of all fields and control stations.
official_conclusion: Unidentified Flying Object cannot be readily explained unless the lighted weather balloon malfunctioned and remained at relatively low altitude.
credibility_notes: Single-witness visual sighting with no radar, photographic, or other sensor corroboration; the observer was rated very reliable but nothing independent supports the account. A lighted weather balloon was launched about 1.6 hours earlier and the report concedes a malfunctioning balloon could explain it. The ascent-rate discrepancy and the pilot's account of maneuvering with the aircraft are unverified, and the pilot's night visual estimates of range and altitude are subjective. Weather was overcast 10/10 per one field, though broken clouds at 3,000 ft with clear above were also reported.

title: DOW-UAP-D174, Utah Ranch Investigation Report, April 2010
summary: A 2010 Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) field investigation report on a Utah ranch near Fort Duchesne, covering deployments of March 22-26 and April 19-23, 2010. It compiles witness interviews about reported creatures ("dog-like" bipedal, "Skinwalker", "little people", pterodactyl-like bird) and orbs/balls of light, along with game cameras, RF sweeps, biosensor plant experiments and DNA analysis of hair samples. The lab results identified the hair samples as raccoon and domestic dog.
key_findings: Eleven independent witnesses reported a bipedal dog-like creature and/or orbs of light near the ranch. Reports range from about 20 years ago to April 2010. | Hair samples collected from barbed-wire fences near reported Skinwalker sightings were DNA-tested: one matched raccoon (Procyon lotor), and three shared a canine HVI sequence common in domestic dogs (9.8-13.8% of random dogs). | BAASS RF sweeps on the mesa recorded unexplained signals at about 1210-1216 MHz and 1232-1238 MHz that were absent the previous day. These fall in bands allocated primarily for military and satellite use, and their origin was not identified. | Witnesses described red, blue, white and golden balls of light that hovered, darted, mimicked vehicle speed or shot straight up. One witness reported facial numbness, warmth and ear ringing when a red ball came within about 4 inches. | Seven Moultrie game cameras and biosensor plant and seed experiments were established. No results were yet available and the plant analysis was explicitly premature.
official_conclusion: No conclusion reached; investigation ongoing. Hair DNA identified as raccoon and domestic dog; RF signal origin requires further research.
credibility_notes: Contractor-produced report built mostly on anecdotal witness testimony, with no sensor corroboration of any UAP. Witnesses are largely redacted, and several accounts are secondhand or are recollections from years or decades ago. The map of creature sightings is acknowledged by the authors as arbitrary extrapolation. Lab DNA results identified the hair samples as raccoon and domestic dog, a mundane explanation. The RF signals fall in known satellite/military bands and were unattributed. Folklore influence (the Skinwalker book) is noted by witnesses themselves. The plant and camera experiments had produced no results at time of writing. The creature and paranormal content is largely outside conventional UAP.
